questions.question_text: What is the prevalence of schizophrenia in people with learning disability?
questions.explanation:
The prevalence rate of schizophrenia is raised threefold over the general population. Most studies report a prevalence of 3 to 3.5 percent for
schizophrenia.

questions.question_text: Angelman syndrome is characterised by
questions.explanation: Angelman syndrome: Epilepsy is seen in 90% of cases and children have severe/profound degree of learning disability.

questions.question_text: Which one of the following statements about Fragile X syndrome is not correct?

options.text: Accounts for 10-12% of mental retardation in males
The genetic abnormality is caused by abnormal trinucleotide CGG repeat at a fragile site on the Y chromosome
Associated with reduced volume of cerebellar vermis

correct_answer.text: The genetic abnormality is caused by abnormal trinucleotide CGG repeat at a fragile site on the Y chromosome

questions.explanation:
Fragile X syndrome is the most common inherited cause of learning disability. The penetrance is greater in males than females. The fragile X
mental retardation 1 (FMR-1) gene is responsible for fragile X syndrome caused by abnormal trinucleotide CGG repeat at a fragile site on the
X chromosome (Xq27.3). Hippocampal size may be increased in some patients, and cerebellar vermis size is reportedly reduced. 
Ref: Hessl, D., Rivera, S. M., & Reiss, A. L. (2004). The neuroanatomy and neuroendocrinology of fragile X syndrome. Mental retardation and
developmental disabilities research reviews, 10(1), 17-24.; Reiss AL, Lee J, Freund L. Neuroanatomy of fragile X syndrome: the temporal
lobe. Neurology 1994; 44: 1317-1324.

questions.question_text: Autism is most commonly associated with
questions.explanation:
About 75% of children with autism have a learning disability. There is also an increased association with epilepsy, tuberous sclerosis,
congenital rubella syndrome, Phenylketonuria and co-morbidity with ADHD, OCD, Anxiety, depression and tic disorders. Ref: New Oxford
Textbook of psychiatry; Second edition; Pg-1852

questions.question_text: Asperger's syndrome is characterised by delays in
questions.explanation:
Asperger's syndrome is characterised by impairments in social interaction, and restricted interests and behaviours seen in autism, but its
early developmental course is characterised by no signi�cant delays in spoken or receptive language.

questions.question_text: Which one among the following features is seen in hands of patients with Down's syndrome?

options.text: Short broad hands with a single palmar crease

questions.explanation:
Children with Down syndrome show hypotonia, oblique palpebral �ssures, abundant neck skin, a small, �attened skull, high cheekbones and
a protruding tongue. High-arched palate and a single palmar crease (simian crease) with syndactyly (webbed �ngers), and altered
dermatoglyphics is also noted.

questions.question_text:
A 5-year-old boy with a severe learning disability has a round face with hypertelorism slanting palpebral �ssures, broad �at nose and has an
infantile cat-like cry. Which one of the following condition is he most likely to su�er from?
questions.explanation:
Cri-du-chat syndrome is characterised by partial deletion 5p region 15.2. The infant has a characteristic cry like a kitten (infantile cat-like cry).
Pronounced microcephaly, Round face with hypertelorism, epicanthic folds, slanting palpebral �ssures, broad �at nose, low-set ears,
micrognathia and dental malocclusion are other notable features. Severe to profound mental retardation, hyperactivity, stereotypes, and
self-injury are the behavioural manifestations.Cornish, K and Bramble, D. Cri du chat syndrome: genotype-phenotype correlations and
recommendations for clinical management Developmental Medicine and Child Neurology 2002, 44: 494-497.

questions.question_text: What is the prevalence of depression among subjects with a learning disability?
questions.explanation:
The prevalence of depression is around 2-4%. Depressed mood and vegetative symptoms are the most striking symptoms, even though
complaints of depression are not always expressed. A depressive mood is not verbalized, particularly among individuals at a lower
intelligence level, but may well be observable.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is classi�ed as a Speci�c Learning Disability?
questions.explanation:
Speci�c Learning Disabilities are considered to be developmental disorders that a�ect the way information is received or processed by the
brain. The most common of these is dyslexia. Conditions such as dyspraxia and dyscalculia are also considered as speci�c learning
disabilities.

questions.question_text:
Prior to the introduction of DSM-5, a multiaxial system was used by DSM-IV . DSM-IV coded mental retardation on which of the following
axes?
questions.explanation: Axis II is for personality disorders or mental retardation.

questions.question_text: The criteria for clinically signi�cant challenging behaviour would include all except

options.text: Behaviour requires intervention by sta� at least once a week
Behaviour has caused more than minor injuries at some times
Behaviour has caused over a few minutes disruption on a weekly basis
Behaviour has caused over a few minutes' disruption at least daily
Behaviours that caused damage that could not be recti�ed

correct_answer.text: Behaviour has caused over a few minutes disruption on a weekly basis

questions.explanation:
Criteria for clinically signi�cant challenging behaviour is given by – 1. At some time, the behaviour has caused more than minor injuries to
themselves or others, or destroyed their immediate living or working environment. 2. At least weekly the behaviours require intervention by
sta�; placed them in physical danger; caused damage that could not be recti�ed; caused at least 1hr of disruption. 3. Behaviour has caused
over a few minutes' disruption at least daily. 4. Severe mental retardation and challenging behaviours: designing high-quality services
(Chapman and Hall, London. Qureshi H (1994) The size of the problem)

questions.question_text:
Which of the following categories of learning disability is more commonly associated with disruptive behaviours and misconduct than the
others listed ?
questions.explanation:
Epidemiological surveys indicate that up to two-thirds of children and adults with mental retardation have comorbid mental disorders. The
prevalence of psychopathology seems to be correlated with the severity of mental retardation; the more severe the mental retardation, the
higher the risk for other mental disorders which would include mood disorders, schizophrenia, attention-de�cit/hyperactivity disorder
(ADHD), and conduct disorder. Disruptive and conduct disorder behaviours occurred more commonly in the mildly retarded group. Those
with severe mental retardation have a particularly high rate of autistic disorder and pervasive developmental disorders.

questions.question_text:
A 25-year-old gentleman with severe learning disability presents to the outpatient clinic with his live-in carer who mentioned that he
indulges in repetitive self-injurious behaviour for no apparent reasons. There is no evidence of clinical depression. Which drug is particularly
helpful in this situation?
questions.explanation:
Opiate antagonists (e.g. Naltrexone) may be e�ective in the treatment of repetitive self-injury. It may decrease self-injurious behaviour
acutely, but it is less e�ective in the long term.

questions.question_text:
You are seeing a 50-year-old man with Down's syndrome in the learning disability clinic. He may be developing Alzheimer's disease. Which of
the following tests would be most useful in establishing a diagnosis?

options.text: Dementia questionnaire for persons with mental retardation
Cambridge examination for mental disorders of the elderly

correct_answer.text: Dementia questionnaire for persons with mental retardation

questions.explanation:
Alzheimer's dementia is relatively common among adults with Down's syndrome and tends to manifest relatively early. Unfortunately,
screening methods used for the detection of dementia in the general population are not suitable for people with intellectual disabilities
because of �oor e�ects. Therefore, direct neuropsychological tests, including the Mini-Mental State Examination are not useful for this
population. Therefore, an observer-rated screening instrument, which is primarily based on the reporting of behavioral changes following
the onset of dementia, is desirable. The two dementia screening instruments that are currently in wide use among people with intellectual
disabilities are the Dementia Scale for Down Syndrome and the Dementia Questionnaire for Persons with Mental Retardation

questions.question_text: Which drug is licensed for the control of aggressive behaviour or intentional self-harm in patients with a learning disability?
Which of the following is correct concerning fragile X syndrome and IQ in males?

options.text: Length of triplet repeats is inversely related to the IQ
Abstract reasoning abilities are higher than expected during adolescence
IQ stabilises around 20-30 yrs of age
Cognitive degeneration is characteristic of the disease

correct_answer.text: Length of triplet repeats is inversely related to the IQ

questions.explanation:
The higher the triplets, the lower the IQ. A drop in IQ is noted especially in males with Fragile X. This is most pronounced between ages 8-12
and stabilises by puberty (age 15). No further drop occurs after this, and, in fact, the adaptive skills improve continuously in most males.
Hence, FXMR cannot be classed as a degenerative disease. The IQ drop phenomenon may be related to higher stress upon abstract abilities
in di�erent IQ tests used for adults and adolescents compared to children. Being concrete thinkers, most FXMR males show a drop in IQ.
This drop is correlated with methylation status of FMR1 gene.

questions.question_text: Which one among the following is not a feature of Cornelia De Lange syndrome?
questions.explanation:
Cornelia de Lange syndrome is characterized by self-injurious behaviour. It is related to lack of pregnancy-associated plasma protein A
(PAPPA) linked to chromosome 9q33; similar phenotype is also associated with Trisomy 5p, ring chromosome 3 (possible association with
3q26.3). It is relatively rare (1/40,000-1/100,000 live births). Patients show continuous eyebrows, hypertrichosis (hirsutism, long eyelashes),
thin down-turned upper lip, prominent philtrum, small upturned nose, downturned mouth, anteverted nostrils, high arched palate and low
set ears. The children also show microcephaly, short stature, small hands and feet, malformed upper limbs, failure to thrive, self-injury,
limited speech in severe cases, language delays, avoidance of being held, stereotypic movements, twirling, severe to profound mental
retardation associated with GI problems, congenital heart defects, visual and hearing problems, skin problems, epilepsy, and death in
infancy. Behavioural problems include feeding di�culties, sleep disturbance, self-injury, temper tantrums, mood disorders, and autistic
features.

questions.question_text: Anxiety is a common association in the following disorders except
questions.explanation:
Some genetic causes of LD have associations with anxiety. For example, Fragile X syndrome is associated with social anxiety disorder,
Prader-Willi syndrome and Rubinstein-Taybi are associated with OCD (Levitas and Read 1998), Williams syndrome is associated with anxiety
disorder and phobias (Ein�eld et al. 2001) while Cornelia De Lange syndrome is associated with compulsive behaviour (Hyman et al. 2001).

questions.question_text: Self-talk seems to be particularly common in children with
questions.explanation:
Parents of individuals with Down syndrome often report that their children engage in self-talk or 'private speech'. Self-talk may be employed
to analyse and think about situations, express inner feelings, or simply as a means to entertain themselves.

questions.question_text: What percentage of patients with learning disability su�ers from a severe form of mental retardation?
questions.explanation:
Mild mental retardation (IQ range, 50 to 70) represents approximately 85 percent of persons with mental retardation. Moderate mental
retardation (IQ range, 35-50) represents about 10 percent of persons with mental retardation. Severe mental retardation (IQ range, 20-35)
comprises about 4 percent of individuals with mental retardation. Profound mental retardation (IQ range below 20) constitutes
approximately 1 to 2 percent of persons with mental retardation. Most individuals with profound mental retardation have identi�able
causes for their condition.

questions.question_text: The prevalence of epilepsy among patients with a learning disability is about
questions.explanation:
Epilepsy is commonly associated with numerous causes of LD e.g. Down's syndrome (5-10%), fragile X (25%), Angelman syndrome (90%), Rett
syndrome (90%).

questions.question_text: Which of the following features is NOT suggestive of Lennox Gestaut syndrome?

options.text: Di�use slow interictal spike waves in waking EEG
Most often appears between ages of 2 and 6

questions.explanation:
Lennox-Gastaut syndrome (LGS), also known as Lennox syndrome, is a resistant form of childhood-onset epilepsy. It mostly appears
between the second and sixth year of life and is characterized by frequent seizures of various types, along with mental retardation and a
progressive reduction in IQ. The seizures may occur everyday. The most frequently occurring seizure is a nocturnal tonic seizure (90%);
followed by myoclonic seizures. Further the presence of non-convulsive status epilepticus characterized by dizziness, apathy and
unresponsiveness is also a feature of LGS seen in ~50% of su�erers. EEG shows spike-wave complexes.

questions.question_text: A patient has autistic traits, litanic and jovial speech but poor eye contact. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
In patients with the fragile X syndrome, there is usually some degree of social impairment with social anxiety and avoidance of eye-to-eye
contact, but with social responsiveness. Jocular speech, up and downs of pitch (Litanic speech), palilalia (repeating the last phrase they have
spoken over and over again) are also seen.

questions.question_text: Which of the following characterises sleep pattern seen in Rett's syndrome?
questions.explanation: In Rett's syndrome unusual sleep characterised by excessive daytime sleep, reduced nocturnal sleep and increased total sleep time is seen.

questions.question_text: Which of the following suggests a subcultural rather than a biological cause for learning disability?

options.text: Equal distribution across families of di�erent types of socio-economic status.
Intellectual ability is impaired in family members
Moderate/ severe impairment in intellectual abilities
Men are more commonly a�ected than females

correct_answer.text: Intellectual ability is impaired in family members

questions.explanation:
The concept of subcultural handicap was introduced by E. O. Lewis (1933). He classi�ed cases of mental de�ciency into the pathological and
the subcultural types. Subcultural refers to the lower extreme variant of the normal IQ distribution seen in the population. The biological or
pathological type is seen to be evenly distributed across all social classes, where as the subcultural type is often seen in social class V, and
associated with mild rather than profound disability. As a result, impaired intellectual ability in family members is often suggestive of a
subcultural form.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is the most common predisposing factor for developing learning disabilities?
questions.explanation: Defects in embryonic development seem to be the most common aetiology of learning disabilities with Down's syndrome leading the list.

questions.question_text: Among the learning disabled population, pica is more commonly seen in which of the following conditions?
questions.explanation:
Pica is a common problem in LD. It is seen more in children than adults with LD. In a survey of adults with LD, the overall prevalence of pica
was between 10-20% in hospital / care units and around 5% in the community. Being male (M:F = 1.4:1), having poor cognitive functioning,
autism, and being non-verbal were associated with a higher odds of having pica, whereas good level of activities of daily living (ADL) was a
protective factor.

questions.question_text: One of the following techniques is used to treat stuttering
questions.explanation:
Stuttering can be treated by Speech and language Therapists who employ a technique called prolonged speech. In this approach, a set of
new speech patterns is taught to the child that can produce changes in the phrasing and articulation of speech and associated respiratory
patterns.

questions.question_text: Which of the following conditions is associated with skin picking?
questions.explanation:
Children with PWS often have an obsession with food, with an insatiable appetite (often a diagnostic feature) with hyperphagia, obesity, skin
picking, impulsivity, aggression, and obsessive-compulsive behaviour.

questions.question_text:
A 43-year-old elderly primi was worried about having a baby with Down syndrome has come to see you for advice. What is the chance of her
delivering a child with Down syndrome?
questions.explanation:
The overall incidence of Down syndrome is approximately 1 in 700 live births, although a further 50% result in a spontaneous abortion and
20% are stillborn. Incidence increases with maternal age, so at 20 years of age a mother has a 1 in 1500 chance of delivering a child with
downs syndrome but this is increased to a 1 in 50 chance at 43 years of age. Ref; Core Psychiatry: ed. Wright, Stern and Phelan Pg 162

questions.question_text:
You are counselling a mother who has one child with autism and is expecting her second. She wishes to know the risk of autism in this
second child. The correct answer is
questions.explanation:
The risk of autism in a sibling of an autistic child is estimated to be less than 10%, provided only one child in the family has autism so far. If
more than one child has autism, the next (expected) child has nearly 35% risk.
Szatmari reported sibling risk for autism to range from 2% to 6% (average 2.2%). When other PDD diagnoses are included, the sibling risk
increases to 5.5%. The risk of autism for second-degree relatives is 0.18%, and 0.12% for third-degree relatives. 70% of the monozygotic (MZ)
twins were concordant for autism, whereas none of the dizygotic (DZ) twins were concordant in a small UK sample. When autistic spectrum
is broadly de�ned, concordance increased to 87% for MZ and to 9% for DZ twins. Szattmari P, Jones MB. Genetic epidemiology of autism and
pervasive developmental disorders. In: FR Volkmar (ed), Cambridge University Press, 2006.

questions.question_text: Which one among the following sex disorders is caused by sex chromosomal monosomy?
questions.explanation: Turner's syndrome is a sex chromosome monosomy. The karyotype 45, XO (i.e. phenotypically female) is observed.

questions.question_text: Which of the following chromosomal abnormalities is most likely to cause mental retardation?
questions.explanation:
An extra chromosome 21 is the most common genetic abnormality found in Down syndrome, and it is most likely to cause mental
retardation. XO is  seen inTurner 's syndrome; XXY in Klinefelter's syndrome, and XXXY in Klinefelter's syndrome variants. These are not
always associated with mental retardation and some children with Turner 's syndrome have normal to superior intelligence. Ref:  Core
psychiatry- ed: Wright, Stern and Phelan Pg 163

questions.question_text: Which of the following is a behavioural phenotype more commonly found in Prader-Willi syndrome?
questions.explanation:
The behavioural phenotypes commonly seen in Prader-Willi syndrome include insatiable appetite and incessant skin picking (80% of cases).
The insistence of routines and compulsive behaviours are commonly reported.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is a postnatal factor that increases the risk of learning disability?
questions.explanation:
Postnatal factors are those occurring in the �rst year of life. CNS infections, intracranial tumours, hypoxic brain injury, head injury (e.g. RTAs,
household accidents, child abuse), exposure to toxic agents are notable factors. The psychosocial environment leading to childhood
deprivation has also been implicated in mild learning disability. Factors such as family instability, frequent moves, and multiple but
inadequate caretakers may deprive an infant of necessary emotional relationships, leading to failure to thrive and potential risk to the
developing brain.

questions.question_text: Those with Down syndrome who survive into their 40s and 50s show pathological brain changes similar to
questions.explanation:
CNS abnormalities seen in Downs syndrome would include reduced brain weight, reduced gyri�cation and cortical thinning, reduced
neuronal numbers in locus cereleus, basal forebrain, cerebellum with reduced cholinergic neurones and neuropathological changes similar
to AD (in those over 40-50 yrs). Post-mortem studies of those with Down syndrome over the age of 40 have shown a high incidence of senile
plaques and neuro�brillary tangles, as seen in Alzheimer's disease. Neuro�brillary tangles are known to occur in a variety of degenerative
diseases, whereas senile plaques seem to be found most often in Alzheimer's disease and in Down syndrome.

questions.question_text: Lesch-Nyhan syndrome is characterised by
questions.explanation:
Lesch-Nyhan syndrome is an X-linked recessive condition. A defect in hypoxanthine guanine phosphoribosyl-transferase with accumulation
of uric acid is noted. Compulsive self-mutilation, which is very distressing to these children is seen. These children often prefer imposed
restraint.

questions.question_text: In which of the following conditions microcephaly is a characteristic feature?
questions.explanation:
Microcephaly, short stature, midface hypoplasia, short palpebral �ssure, thin upper lip, retrognathia in infancy, micrognathia in adolescence,
hypo plastic long or smooth philtrum are noted in foetal alcohol syndrome. Mild to moderate mental retardation, irritability, inattention,
memory impairment are also seen.

questions.question_text: The most common inherited cause of Learning disability is
questions.explanation:
The most common inherited cause of LD is Fragile X syndrome. This syndrome a�ects approximately 1 in 4425 to 6045 males and causes
mental retardation in 1 in 8000 females with an X-linked dominant transmission.

questions.question_text: All of the following are true when comparing high-functioning autism (HFA) with Asperger's Disorder except

options.text: IQ levels of the two groups are comparable
Di�erences in language between these groups reduce with age
Language onset is delayed for HFA but not Asperger's
High functioning autism is more common in girls while Asperger's is more common in boys
There is little evidence to support the retention of two diagnostic categories

correct_answer.text: High functioning autism is more common in girls while Asperger's is more common in boys

questions.explanation:
Both HFA and Asperger's syndrome are more common in boys. Macintosh and Dissanayake (2004) noted that although di�erent language
patterns were evident (the HFA group demonstrating more atypical speech patterns [later speech onset, echolalia, noun reversals, atypical
gestures], while the Asperger 's group tended to have more verbal rituals and asked odd questions), studies demonstrated little basis for
di�erentiation on the basis of diagnosis. Although the HFA group demonstrated greater dysfunction in preschool, by adolescence, the only
distinguishing feature between these two groups was that the teens with Asperger 's disorder engaged in more pedantic dialogues.

questions.question_text: Which of the following statements is correct about velocardiofacial syndrome?

options.text: Large ears and wide palpebral �ssures are important physical features
It is usually associated with severe learning disabilities
It occurs in around 1 in 4500 people
It is usually associated with cognitive impairment and dementia

correct_answer.text: It occurs in around 1 in 4500 people

questions.explanation:
The velocardiofacial syndrome also known as Di-George's syndrome is a congenital disorder caused by a microdeletion of chromosome 22
at band q11.2. It has an estimated incidence of 1 in 4000 to 5000 births. The features are collectively referred to as CATCH-22, which includes
Cardiac defects, Abnormal facies, Thymic hypoplasia, Cleft palate and Hypocalcemia due to chromosomal 22q11.2 deletion. Mental
retardation and learning disabilities are common. A high rate of psychiatric morbidity is reported in VCFS patients, with schizophrenia and
bipolar disorder being most commonly reported.  
Ref: Tezenas Du Montcel S, Mendizabai H, Ayme S, Levy A, Philip N. Prevalence of 22q11 microdeletion. J Med Genet 1996;33:719.

questions.question_text: Which one of the following conditions is most likely to be associated with hypertrichosis and severe learning disability?
questions.explanation:
Cornelia de Lange syndrome is characterized by self-injurious behaviour. It is related to lack of pregnancy-associated plasma protein A
(PAPPA) linked to chromosome 9q33; similar phenotype is also associated with Trisomy 5p, ring chromosome 3 (possible association with
3q26.3). It is relatively rare (1/40,000-1/100,000 live births). Patients show continuous eyebrows, hypertrichosis (hirsutism, long eyelashes),
thin down turning upper lip, prominent philtrum, small upturned nose, downturned mouth, anteverted nostrils, high arched palate and low
set ears. The children also show microcephaly, short stature, small hands and feet, malformed upper limbs, failure to thrive, self-injury,
limited speech in severe cases, language delays, avoidance of being held, stereotypic movements, twirling, severe to profound mental
retardation associated with GI problems, congenital heart defects, visual and hearing problems, skin problems, epilepsy, and death in
infancy. Behavioural problems include feeding di�culties, sleep disturbance, self-injury, temper tantrums, mood disorders, and autistic
features.

questions.question_text: Which of the following diseases is inherited in an autosomal dominant manner?
questions.explanation:
San�lippo disease and Hurler's syndrome are autosomal recessive conditions. Lesch-Nyhan syndrome and Hunter's syndrome and X-linked
recessive conditions. Tuberous sclerosis, while in most cases the result of a spontaneous mutation, follows an autosomal dominant pattern
when inherited.

questions.question_text: In which of the following syndromes of learning disability is anxiety disorder most common?
questions.explanation: In Fragile X syndrome, presentation with anxiety is very common.

questions.question_text: Happy disposition and paroxysmal laughter are features commonly seen in
questions.explanation: Angelman syndrome is characterized by puppet-like gait, attraction to water, happy disposition, and laughing at minimal provocation.

questions.question_text: Deletion of the paternal 15q12 chromosomal segment causes
questions.explanation:
Prader-Willi syndrome is associated with a deletion in 15q12 of paternal origin; 75% cases are due to this deletion of paternally derived
chromosome 15, but 25% is due to maternal uniparental disomy. M:F = 4:3. It is seen in 1/10,000 of live births, 90% cases being sporadic in
the absence of family history. The candidate gene is a small nuclear ribonucleoprotein polypeptide (SNRPN).

questions.question_text: Predisposing factors for behavioural problems in children with LD includes
questions.explanation:
Various predisposing factors for behavioural problems in children with LD includes sensory disabilities, poor communication, epilepsy,
physical illness-ear infections, dental problems and constipation, medication, presence of limited range of coping strategies,and a history of
abuse.

questions.question_text: 20% of patients with autism have one of the following features
questions.explanation:
Epidemiological surveys have shown that the prevalence rates of learning disability in children with autism is around 40% (e.g., Chakrabarti
& Fombonne, 2001). Obesity is estimated to be around 20%.

questions.question_text: Klinefelter syndrome is characterised by all except
questions.explanation:
XYY (extra-Y), rather than XXY composition (Klinefelter's syndrome) is overrepresented in the prison population. More the number of Y
chromosomes, higher the incidence of aggression.

questions.question_text: What is the mode of inheritance of Fragile X syndrome?
questions.explanation:
Fragile X syndrome is the most common inherited cause of learning disability, with X-linked dominant transmission. The penetrance is low
but greater in males than females, due to the protective e�ects of second normal X chromosome in females.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is true about the epidemiology of autism?

options.text: More common in children who have had the MMR vaccine
More common in girls than boys
More common in parents of higher socio-economic status
Monozygotic twin concordance is greater than 90%

questions.explanation:
Twin studies report 60% concordance for classic autism in monozygotic (MZ) twins versus 0% in dizygotic (DZ) twins. If a broader autistic
phenotype that included communication and social disorders is considered, the concordance increases remarkably from 60% to 92% in MZ
twins and from 0% to 10% in DZ pairs. This translates to 90% heritability.

questions.question_text: Self-injurious behaviour occurs most frequently between the ages of
questions.explanation:
Repetitive or stereotypical acts that produce self-in�icted injury (self-injurious behaviour) occur in 20% of adults with learning disability and
up to 50% of those requiring institutional care. Self-injurious behaviours occur more often among persons with moderate and severe mental
retardation (IQ < 50); most frequently between the ages of 10 and 30, with a peak between 15 and 20 years of age. It occurs most commonly
in males and those with impairments in vision, hearing, mobility and communication. It is also seen commonly in patients with a history of
epilepsy and autism. The occurrence of self-injurious behaviour is related to genetic and organic disturbances and adverse environmental
and developmental conditions. Certain psychiatric disorders such as depression may also elicit self-injurious behaviour. It most commonly
takes the form of head banging, banging other body parts, pinching, biting, scratching, hair pulling, and pica.

questions.question_text: Which one of the following is the most common chromosomal aberration seen in Down syndrome?

options.text: Mosaicism with both normal and trisomic cells present
Mosaicism with only trisomic cells present

questions.explanation:
Down syndrome is the most common genetic cause of LD. It results from trisomy of chromosome 21. Full trisomy 21 (non-disjunction)
occurs in ~95% of cases. Robertsonian translocations are seen in ~5% (of which ~45% show fusion usually between 14 and 21). Mosaicism (a
mixture of normal and trisomic cell lines) is noted in 2-5% of all cases.

questions.question_text: Which one among the following is an X-linked recessive condition?
questions.explanation:
Hunter's syndrome is rare and is seen in around 1/100,000 live-births. It is an X-linked recessive condition linked to iduronate sulfatase
de�ciency (locus X q28)

questions.question_text: Which of the following is most likely to be true while diagnosing PTSD in patients with learning disability?

options.text: Aggression may be the most common presenting problem.
Never needs a history of trauma
Remission of symptoms is often within few days

correct_answer.text: Aggression may be the most common presenting problem.

questions.explanation:
In people with learning disabilities, aggression is the most common presenting symptom of post-traumatic stress disorder, as opposed to
sleep problems, nightmares and 'jumpiness', which are commonly reported in the non-disabled population. Doyle & Mitchell (2003) reported
that 16.5% of psychiatric referrals to paediatric learning disability teams meet the criteria for post-traumatic stress disorder. Doyle and
Mitchell, Journal of Intellectual Disabilities 2003; 7; 23

questions.question_text: Which of the following statements is true regarding posttraumatic stress disorder in adults with learning disabilities?

options.text: An exaggerated startle response is often seen
Co-morbid depressive symptoms are less likely than in adults with average intellect
Symptoms resolve within a few weeks following the traumatic event
It is highly likely to be diagnosed in adults with severe learning disabilities

correct_answer.text: An exaggerated startle response is often seen

questions.explanation:
In studies of PTSD in the general adult population with learning disability, the symptoms most commonly reported were nightmares, a
feeling of jumpiness and trouble sleeping (Helzer et al. 1987). In half of those with symptoms, the symptoms lasted less than 6 months, but
for one-third the symptoms persisted for over a year. It is unusual for PTSD to occur in isolation and comorbidity with other psychiatric
disorders is the norm. People with learning disability are at greater risk for the psychiatric disorder than the general population (Rutter at al
1970). Individuals with mild to profound learning disability su�er disorders similar to those a�ecting the general population. The main
di�culty is the diagnosis, as the presentations of a disorder may be di�erent in those with severe developmental delay. Therefore, the
diagnosis of PTSD in those who have a severe learning disability, who do not have the communication skills to describe their thoughts,
feelings and mood may be hindered. At times we are reliant on observing changes in behaviour and function, for example, aggression,
regressive behaviours and changes in sleep pattern. Owing to the limited recognition of PTSD in people with learning disability these
symptoms may be attributed to other psychiatric diagnoses. (Excerpt was retrieved from McCarthy J (2001), PTSD in learning disability

questions.question_text:
You are seeing a 20-year-old gentleman in a nursing home. He has cerebral palsy and history of chronic epilepsy. His communication skills
are very limited. He has limited ability to self-care, cannot contribute partially to self-maintenance under complete supervision and would
need 24-hour nursing care. The severity of his mental retardation could be classi�ed as
questions.explanation:
Patients with profound disability show very limited comprehension and use of language, may achieve very limited self-care, need nursing
care or 'life support' under a carefully planned and structured environment like group-homes. Organic aetiology are often obvious in many
cases with severe neurological and physical disabilities a�ecting mobility being common. Associated problems like epilepsy, visual and
hearing impairment are also common.

questions.question_text: IQ of an 11-year-old boy is evaluated as 75. Which of the following is true?

options.text: Low IQ at age 11 is a de�nite predictor of conduct disorder at a later age
There will be a further drop in IQ after adolescence
There is an increased risk of schizophrenia compared to general population
He falls two percentiles below the average IQ of the standard population

correct_answer.text: There is an increased risk of schizophrenia compared to general population

questions.explanation:
In people with borderline IQ, the risk of schizophrenia is increased. IQ is considered to be relatively age- invariant and borderline IQ at age
11 in itself does not predict a further drop in IQ with age.

questions.question_text: Risk of developing Alzheimer's disease in Down syndrome is increased most by

options.text: Mild learning disability rather than severe learning disability

questions.explanation:
Eczema and anxiety are irrelevant choices, not associated with increased risk of AD in Down syndrome (DS). There is some evidence for
positive family history of dementia increasing risk of clinical expression of AD in DS. For patients with DS, age is the most important risk
factor for AD. A few case studies suggest that persons with DS and atypical karyotypes (partial trisomies, mosaicism, and translocations) may
have a lower risk of AD than patients with full trisomy. In patients with DS, the APOE epsilon 4 allele is associated with increased risk of AD,
and the epsilon e2 allele may be protective. Being male and lacking oestrogen may be other risk factors for earlier AD expression in those
with DS. Note that almost all adults more than 40 with DS will have AD-like neuropathology but only up to 75% have the clinically expressed
AD. The rate of decline following expression of AD may depend on age, and cognitive ability, the less able have more rapid decline (Temple
et al., 2001). But there seems to be no relationship between the level of learning disability and risk of dementia or age at onset of dementia
(Holland et al., 1998).

questions.question_text: The highest incidence of intellectual disabilities is seen in
questions.explanation:
The prevalence of intellectual disabilities at any one time is estimated to range from 1 percent to 3 percent of the population. The incidence
of intellectual disabilities is di�cult to calculate because mild intellectual disability sometimes goes unrecognised until middle childhood. The
highest incidence is in school-age children, with the peak at ages 10 to 14 years. Intellectual disabilities are about 1.5 times more common
among men than among women. Those with severe or profound disabilities have high mortality rates because of the complications of
associated physical disorders.

Obesity, small hands and feet, microorchidism, cryptorchidism (hypogonadism), short stature, almond-shaped eyes, �at face, prominent

questions.question_text: A subcultural rather than a biological explanation for learning disabilities is supported by which of the following observations?

options.text: Normal distribution of learning disability across di�erent socio-economic groups
Lower IQ pro�le in parents and siblings
Presence of moderate or severe learning disability

correct_answer.text: Lower IQ pro�le in parents and siblings

questions.explanation:
The concept of subcultural handicap was introduced by E. O. Lewis (1933). He classi�ed cases of mental de�ciency into the pathological and
the subcultural types. 'Subcultural LD' refers to the lower extreme variant of normal IQ distribution seen in the general population. The
biological or pathological type is seen to be evenly distributed across all social classes, where as the subcultural type is often seen in social
class V, and associated with mild rather than profound disability. Such division has not been supported by later epidemiological studies of
mental retardation. Subcultural LD suggests the concept of a psychosocial causation (e.g. physical and emotional neglect) as there is a
higher incidence of lower IQ pro�le in the families. This is controversial.

questions.question_text: In adults with learning disabilities, dysphagia is a known side e�ect of which of the following drugs?
questions.explanation:
Dysphagia may occur as an e�ect of medications prescribed to a person with learning disability. The most common agents are (1)
medications altering levels of alertness, for example, benzodiazepines (Whyllie et al., 1986). Sedating anticonvulsants or antipsychotics can
also result in dysphagia. (2) Medications altering muscle tone/ co-ordination, for example, baclofen, and benzodiazepines. (3) Antipsychotic
medications that delay swallow process or increase salivation (Hughes et al.,1994, Sokolo� et al.,1997)

questions.question_text: The most common cause of death in Down syndrome is
questions.explanation:
The highest absolute risk of death in Down syndrome is noted below age 1 where congenital heart disease is the predominant cause. But
when all individuals with Down syndrome are considered, irrespective of their age, the overall predominant cause of death is
bronchopneumonia and other related infections.

questions.explanation: Rett's syndrome is supposed to be inherited in an X-linked dominant fashion; it is not seen in males.

questions.question_text:
IQ assessment was carried out on a 7-year-old boy with a history of delayed developmental milestones. His IQ was calculated to be 56. What
level of learning disability is he su�ering from?
questions.explanation:
General intellectual functioning is determined by the use of standardized tests of intelligence, and the term signi�cantly sub-average is
de�ned as an IQ of approximately 70 or below or two standard deviations below the mean for the particular test. Mild LD has IQ range 50-
69, Moderate with a range 35-49, Severe in the range 20-34, and Profound being below 20. Borderline intellectual functioning, according to
DSM-5, is not within the diagnostic boundary of mental retardation and refers to a full-scale IQ in the 71 to 84.

questions.question_text: In males with the fragile X syndrome, which of the following statements is correct?

options.text: The delay in language development is usually unrelated to the degree of intellectual development
The mean IQ score in adulthood is stable with increased age
The mean IQ in a�ected boys is 20 to 30
There is a relationship between the length of the DNA trinucleotide repeat and the level of intelligence

correct_answer.text: There is a relationship between the length of the DNA trinucleotide repeat and the level of intelligence

questions.explanation:
Fragile X syndrome is an X-Linked disorder with an unusual pattern of inheritance. The fragility of the X chromosome is now known to be
associated with an unstable region in the fragile-X mental retardation (FMR-1) gene, which was �rst described in 1991. This region of
unstable DNA increases in length and degree of instability in successive generations ( a pre-mutation) until a critical point is reached, and the
gene no longer functions (a full mutation). The instability is caused by an increase in CGG repeats from the 50 or so repeats that are usual to
50-100 repeats (pre-mutation) to over 230 repeats (full mutation). The chance of a child inheriting a lengthened gene is proportional to the
length of the unstable region in the carrier mother. The severity of the intellectual disability probably depends mostly on the proportion of
cells in which the abnormal chromosome is inactivated, X inactivation being random. The associated intellectual disability is mild to
moderate. (Ref: New oxford textbook of psychiatry-2nd edition, 1840)

questions.question_text:
The Special Education Needs & Disability Act of 2001 (UK) requires schools to draw up accessibility strategies for children with intellectual
disabilities. The aim of this programme is to facilitate

options.text: the inclusion of some pupils without intellectual disabilities to special needs schools
the early provision of special needs education to pupils with intellectual disabilities
the inclusion of pupils with intellectual disabilities to mainstream schools
the enrolment of pupils with intellectual disabilities to special schools
the identi�cation of gifted pupils with high IQ in mainstream schools and provide them special education

correct_answer.text: the inclusion of pupils with intellectual disabilities to mainstream schools

questions.explanation:
Schools are required to draw up which of the accessibility strategies with the aim of facilitating the inclusion of pupils with intellectual
disabilities to mainstream schools and "to make reasonable adjustments so that they are not disadvantaged".

questions.question_text: Which one of the following statements about schizophrenia in individuals with learning disability is incorrect?

options.text: Patients are less likely to have complex delusional ideas
The rate is raised threefold over the general population.
Thought disorder is probably more evident
It is nearly always associated with a change in personality
It is nearly always associated with a reduction in functional abilities

correct_answer.text: Thought disorder is probably more evident

questions.explanation:
Age of onset of schizophrenia in the LD population tends to be earlier (on average 23 years) with few di�erences in symptomatology, except
in severe LD where there may be unexplained aggression, bizarre behaviours, mood lability, or increased mannerisms and stereotypies.
Impulsive, aggressive, and unpredictable behaviours may dominate the clinical picture. Thought disorder and complex persecutory
delusions are probably less evident.

questions.question_text: Which of the following childhood disorders is more common in girls than in boys?
questions.explanation:
Rett disorder occurs exclusively in girls. All others are seen more commonly in boys. Ref; Lewis's Child and Adolescent Psychiatry: A
Comprehensive Textbook, 4th Edition

questions.question_text:

of the following?
questions.explanation:
The risk of having another child with the same syndrome is highest if their �rst child has down's syndrome with Robertsonian translocation.
Other types include Full Trisomy 21, which occurs in 95% of cases and Mosaicism.

questions.question_text: An autosomal recessive pattern of inheritance occurs in
questions.explanation:
Phenylketonuria and Hurler syndrome are autosomal recessive disorders. William syndrome is an autosomal dominant disorder
(Chromosome 7).

questions.question_text:
A 32-year-old patient with learning disability requires lithium for the treatment of his bipolar disorder. Which of the following baseline
investigation must be done before initiating therapy?
questions.explanation:
Lithium is useful in the treatment bipolar a�ective disorder and augmentation of antidepressant therapy and is also helpful in reducing
aggressive outbursts. It is licensed for the 'control of aggressive behaviour or intentional self-harm'. EEG must be obtained as a baseline
along with renal functions and cell counts before lithium is started. This is because even a therapeutic dose of lithium may induce seizures in
those with epilepsy. Patients with pre-existing EEG changes are more prone to lithium toxicity (Frith Prescribing Guidelines p.99)
